title: Crumbs under the table (Mark 7:24–30)
hook: a Syrophoenician mother talks back to Jesus and wins
carry: even the dogs eat the crumbs

segments.voice: Yesterday, what comes out: not what goes in, but what comes from the heart. Your line was from the heart. Did you catch a sharp word before it left? Day one hundred eighty-eight.

Jesus leaves Galilee and goes north, over the border, to the borders of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the coast. He slips into a house and wants nobody to know he's there. It doesn't work: Mark says he could not be hid. A woman finds him. She isn't Jewish, she isn't from his people, and she has no claim on him at all. But her young daughter has an unclean spirit, Mark says, and the mother falls at his feet and begs. What happens next is an uncomfortable conversation, and readers still argue over it. Today: crumbs under the table.
screen: `NORTH, OVER THE BORDER.` → `A HOUSE, AND NO ONE TO KNOW.` → `A MOTHER AT HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Mark tells us exactly who she is: "The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation." Greek-speaking, from the Phoenician coast of Syria. An outsider, in every way that mattered then. And Jesus's answer, in the old King James Bible, is hard to hear: "Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs." The children are Israel. The dogs are everyone else. Mark's Greek uses a small form of the word for dog, the kind kept in the house, but it still stings. And she doesn't walk away. She doesn't argue that she isn't one. She picks up his picture and turns it: "Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs." Fine. Then I'll take the crumbs. Anyone who's watched kids eat knows the dog under the table eats well. And Jesus says, in the King James words: "For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter." She goes home and finds the child lying in bed, well. Christians read this conversation in several ways. Some say Jesus was testing her faith, and she passed. Some say he was voicing what people around him thought, so that her answer would overturn it. Others say plainly that she changed his mind, and that Mark lets us see it. However they read it, the text is clear on one thing: her daughter is healed for this saying, for what the mother said. And notice the word first. Children first, not children only. Right after this, Jesus heads into more Gentile country. The crumbs, it turns out, are about to become a feast.
screen: `A GREEK, A SYROPHOENICIAN.` · `THE CHILDREN'S BREAD, AND THE DOGS.` · `YET THE DOGS EAT THE CRUMBS.` · `CHILDREN FIRST, NOT ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand up for someone you love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love who needs something they can't ask for themselves. A child who needs help at school. A parent navigating doctors. A friend facing a system that keeps saying no. Picture yourself, like this mother, refusing to take the first no as the last word. Respectful, clever, stubborn. What would you say? If you pray, you can bring their need to God as boldly as she did. The bell holds the time.
Crumbs under the table. An outsider mother's reply to Jesus, turning his own picture into a yes for her daughter.
Your line: even the dogs eat the crumbs. Today, don't take the first no for someone you love. Ask again, kindly and cleverly. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Christians look to the Syrophoenician woman as a model of bold, persistent prayer for others, and some churches read her story when speaking about welcome for outsiders.

original.note: Greek: a small form of the word for dog, a house dog. still a sting.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus called someone a dog.
what it means: a Gentile mother takes his hard words and turns them into a yes for her daughter, and wins.
what a scholar hears: kynarion, little dog, and first, not only. readers still disagree whether he tested her or she changed his mind.

notes: Three readings (test; voicing a common view; she changed his mind) given without ranking; the third is contested in some traditions. Keepers should confirm fair.
'The one person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus' is a common observation; confirm.
κυνάριον as a diminutive 'house dog'; many scholars note the diminutive may have lost force in Koine. Stated as 'softer ... but still a sting'. Confirm.
Matthew calls her 'a woman of Canaan'; not mentioned.
